html:
The eruption of Mount Vesuvius, near Naples, in 79 CE, which buried the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum. It is traditionally dated 24 August, though finds suggest it may have been in October.

Pompeii had been shaken by an earthquake in 62 CE and was still being repaired. On the day, a column of ash and pumice rose many kilometres into the sky and rained down on the town for hours. The next morning, surges of hot gas and ash raced down the slopes and killed those who had stayed. Pliny the Elder, commander of the fleet across the bay, died trying to rescue people; his nephew Pliny the Younger watched and described it in two letters.

Dug up from the 1700s on, Pompeii is the best-preserved Roman town: streets, shops, bars, graffiti, wall paintings, and plaster casts of the dead made from the hollows their bodies left in the ash. It shows daily life in the Roman Empire as no text can. Compare the eruption of Thera.
